title: Bolded list-item labels introducing a category
description: This latent activates on the pattern of a bolded (or otherwise emphasized) short header phrase that names a category or item, immediately followed by an explanatory clause elaborating on it, typically as part of an enumerated or bulleted list. It fires on constructions like 'Term**: explanation follows' where the bold label sets up a definition, feature, or characteristic being described. It would not activate on plain prose sentences lacking this label-then-explain list format, nor on list items that are not bolded/headed by a short noun phrase, even if they discuss similar topics like work environments or job features.

title: Implementation intention instructions
description: This latent fires on advice-list items that instruct the reader to form an 'implementation intention'—a concrete plan specifying when and where a task will be performed—typically phrased as a bolded step header followed by a directive to plan specifics. It activates on repeated near-identical formulations of this planning instruction (e.g., 'Plan out when and where you will do the task'), and also extends to adjacent supportive statements about how such planning reduces anxiety or increases comfort, suggesting it captures the broader self-help/behavioral-strategy framing around this specific technique. It would not activate on generic goal-setting advice, motivational statements, or task instructions that lack the specific 'when/where' scheduling framing, nor on discussions of implementation intentions in an abstract, non-instructional (e.g., academic or descriptive) register.

title: Affirming self-worth reassurance
description: This latent fires on formulaic, affirming statements that reassure the reader of their own worth, strength, and deservingness, typically in the syntactic pattern 'You are/deserve to be [strong/capable/loved/respected/happy]' or 'Remember, you deserve/are...'. It activates most strongly on short, templated, second-person affirmations centered on words like 'deserve,' 'worthy,' 'strong,' 'capable,' 'love,' and 'respect,' often opening with imperative cues like 'Remember,' 'You are,' or 'Keep,' and frequently appearing as closing supportive remarks in advice/therapy-style text. It does not activate on general advice-giving, situational analysis, practical suggestions, numbered lists, or empathetic observations about someone else's feelings/situation (e.g., 'It's understandable that...', 'Here are some tips...'), even when these appear in the same supportive-advice context, since those lack the direct affirming '(you) deserve/are worthy/strong' self-esteem framing.

title: Bolded list-item header introducing a suggestion
description: This latent fires on sentences that begin a list item with a short bolded (or otherwise emphasized) category label followed by a colon, then elaborate with a suggestion or recommendation, often naming specific platforms, tools, or brands as examples. It activates on structured, enumerable advice content where the sentence functions as one entry in a broader list (e.g., tips, options, categories). It would not activate on plain prose recommendations lacking the header/colon list format, nor on narrative or explanatory sentences that don't serve as an itemized entry introducing a sub-topic.

title: Naming a recurring interpersonal grievance
description: This latent activates on statements where a speaker calls out a recurring, pattern-based behavior from another person that causes mild frustration or hurt feelings, often as a lead-in to a conversation about relationship dynamics ('I've noticed that when X, Y usually happens'). It responds to first-person observational framing of a repeated negative pattern in interpersonal communication, typically involving timing, responsiveness, or reliability. It would not activate on one-off complaints, general statements of fact, third-person narration, or descriptions of behavior that lack the 'noticed pattern + mild grievance' framing directed at a specific relationship.

title: List-item and enumeration markers
description: This latent fires on the structural tokens that introduce items in an enumerated list or advice sequence—numerals like '2.' or '3.' at the start of a list item, and connective/lead-in words like 'By', 'Consider', or 'By communicating' that begin a clause explaining a method or step. It activates most strongly on bare enumeration markers (numbers followed by a period) and on short sentence-initial fragments that frame an upcoming recommendation or rationale, and more weakly on fuller sentences within advice-giving text that still carry this list-structuring or step-framing function. It does not activate on ordinary declarative or descriptive sentences that lack list/step structure or a 'by [doing X]' framing, even if they discuss similar advice-giving content, since the latent tracks the formatting/discourse-structuring cue rather than the topical substance of the advice.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral or digit that begins an item in an enumerated list (e.g., '3.', '4. **', '9'), regardless of the list's topic or the content that follows. It activates most strongly on the bare number/marker token itself, especially in structured advice or step-by-step responses (tips, suggestions, compromises, steps to consider). It does not activate on the prose content of list items, bullet points marked with asterisks alone without a leading number, or ordinary sentences lacking an enumerated list structure.

title: Formulaic exclamatory framing of a dilemma
description: This latent fires on short, stock exclamatory openers that dramatically frame an upcoming discussion of a tricky, emotional, or difficult situation (e.g., 'The age-old dilemma!', 'What a complicated situation!', 'The drama!', 'Oh boy, this is a tough one!'), as well as brief empathetic acknowledgment phrases ('I totally get it!', 'I completely understand!') and greetings ('Hello there!') that serve the same rhetorical role of a canned, upbeat conversational preamble before substantive advice. It activates most strongly on these templated, punchy, exclamation-marked micro-sentences that function as rhetorical throat-clearing or framing devices rather than conveying content themselves. It does NOT activate strongly on the actual substantive advice-giving sentences that follow such openers -- e.g., detailed reasoning, suggestions, conditional judgments, or empathetic statements embedded in longer explanatory text -- even when they reference similar topics like 'complex situation' or 'dilemma' in a non-exclamatory, discursive sentence.

title: Moral verdict on someone's behavior
description: This latent fires on short, declarative judgment sentences that pronounce a verdict on a specific person's (often possessive-marked, e.g. 'Your mom's', 'Susan's', 'D's') reaction or behavior, typically using evaluative adjectives like unacceptable, unreasonable, unfair, entitled, disproportionate, or problematic. It activates most strongly on terse, formulaic AITA-style summary statements that name an actor and deliver a blunt moral assessment of their conduct, and also weakly on standalone list-numeral tokens (2., 3., 4.) that likely precede such verdict statements in enumerated advice lists. It does not activate on longer advice, explanations, hedged reasoning, questions, or descriptive narrative sentences that lack a direct evaluative verdict about a named party's behavior, even if they discuss similar interpersonal conflict topics.
